items.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] The list of people you’ve played with since then is most impressive: Gerry Mulligan you played with... [INTERVIEWEE] Yup, yup.

ctx.x: Melodiousness. That’s worse. We know what you mean.

But his melodic thinking. And he had a different approach than Ray did of course. But I liked lines that really tied together, that really expressed an idea, that didn’t have to stop halfway through because technically you couldn’t find the next note you were trying to say. Even if it’s simple, just real notes. I mean like Gerry Mulligan, listen to Gerry Mulligan. What makes him outstanding is he learned to use the lower register. And he understood the sonic thing on the baritone, and so he played melodies on the…

nobody else quite played. He had a melodiousness to his playing that it just comes through every time you hear — you hear two seconds you know it’s Gerry Mulligan on the baritone, because there’s a sonar — I don’t know any words. Buy a dictionary and learn words like sonorous, melodicness, melodiciticity, melodocity — and use them. So some day, when you do an interview you —
